patient.name: Ellie Brennan
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the ENT emergency clinic
patient.complaint: Severe sore throat, fever and painful swallowing for 3 days
background: Second-year law student living in halls in Waterloo
Her flatmate had a sore throat last week
Four sore throats needing antibiotics in the past year

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a sore throat, fever and exudate: count the Centor criteria, and watch for trismus and a hot potato voice (quinsy) or splenomegaly (glandular fever).

points: Ellie, 20, has a **severe sore throat** for 3 days.
Swallowing hurts so much she is barely eating.
Headache, aches and feeling hot and shivery.
Her flatmate was ill with a sore throat last week.

steps.lead: Ellie's palatine tonsils are inflamed. Most cases are **viral**, but her picture raises the question of **Group A Streptococcus**.
Ellie fits the age group (**young adult**) and has close **contact** with an infected flatmate in halls.

points: Both tonsils are **red, swollen and covered in white exudate**.
**Tender anterior cervical lymph nodes** on both sides.
Uvula central; she opens her mouth fully; voice normal.

steps.lead: Ellie has the full set: severe sore throat, **odynophagia**, fever over 38°C, exudate and tender anterior nodes.
Score Ellie with the **Centor criteria**: exudate, tender anterior nodes, fever over 38°C and no cough.

visual.title: Ellie's Centor score
visual.label: Ellie 4/4
visual.caption: One point each: exudate, tender anterior nodes, fever over 38°C, absence of cough.

steps.q: Ellie scores 4/4 on Centor with no splenomegaly. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: A **Centor of 4** makes **Group A strep tonsillitis** most likely. Glandular fever gives splenomegaly and posterior nodes; viral pharyngitis usually has a cough.

points: Day 6: the pain shifts to the **left side** and gets worse.
Muffled '**hot potato**' voice; she is drooling.
Uvula pushed to the right by a swollen left soft palate.

steps.lead: Ellie now has the emergency features of a **peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**: one-sided pain, **trismus**, hot potato voice and a tender peritonsillar swelling.

steps.text: Quinsy pushes the **uvula away** from the abscess. Bilateral symmetrical tonsils with a central uvula is tonsillitis, not quinsy.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical with Centor), or a throat swab when you need to confirm Group A strep.

steps.q: Ellie scores Centor 4. What confirms Group A strep if needed?
steps.r: Tonsillitis is a **clinical diagnosis**; a **throat swab** confirms Group A strep when a bacterial cause is suspected. Monospot is for glandular fever.

steps.lead: Ellie's diagnosis is **clinical**, scored with Centor. A **throat swab** would confirm Group A strep but does not delay treatment.

steps.title: Ellie's bloods on day 6 (ENT clinic)
steps.text: Raised neutrophils and CRP support a **bacterial** infection, now with a collection.

visual.title: Ellie's temperature
visual.caption: Improving on penicillin, then a new spike with one-sided pain: the quinsy. It settles after drainage.

steps.text: If the stem adds **splenomegaly** or posterior nodes in a teenager, the investigation is a **Monospot** for glandular fever, not a throat swab.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where Centor decides antibiotics (phenoxymethylpenicillin; clarithromycin if allergic), a dehydrated child is admitted, and quinsy needs drainage plus antibiotics.

steps.lead: Ellie's **Centor of 4** is above 3, so she gets **phenoxymethylpenicillin** (penicillin V) for 5-10 days with paracetamol and ibuprofen.

steps.q: Which antibiotic is first-line for Ellie, who has no allergy?
steps.r: **Phenoxymethylpenicillin**. Amoxicillin is avoided because it causes a widespread rash if the sore throat is actually glandular fever.

steps.title: Sore throat decisions
nodes: Systemically unwell or cannot drink? → admit
steps.caption: Emergencies first; then the score decides antibiotics.

steps.lead: On day 6 Ellie's **quinsy** needs **drainage plus antibiotics**, with a corticosteroid as an adjunct. A child unable to drink would be admitted whatever the Centor.

points: ENT aspirate 4 mL of pus from the left peritonsillar space.
IV benzylpenicillin and a single dose of dexamethasone.
Next morning she is swallowing and opening her mouth.

steps.lead: Ellie takes no statin. But if a penicillin-allergic patient on **atorvastatin** needs **clarithromycin**, hold the statin: the combination risks **rhabdomyolysis**.

visual.title: Tonsillitis episodes in the last 12 months
visual.label: Ellie 5
visual.caption: Ellie has 5 this year, so she meets the criteria only if she also had 5+ last year.

steps.lead: Ellie's recurrent episodes are counted against the **SIGN criteria**: 7+ in 1 year, 5+ in each of 2 years, or 3+ in each of 3 years.
Ellie's care uses the **Centor criteria** to decide antibiotics and the **SIGN** tonsillectomy criteria for her recurrent episodes.

steps.text: One quinsy plus recurrent tonsillitis is a common reason for tonsillectomy, but the exam answer for an acute quinsy is **drainage plus antibiotics**, not immediate tonsillectomy.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the organism (Group A strep), why bacterial tonsillitis looks different, molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever, or why quinsy causes trismus.

steps.lead: Ellie's tonsils are lymphoid tissue in **Waldeyer's ring**, the first immune checkpoint for what she breathes and swallows.
Ellie's high fever and exudate come from GAS virulence factors (**streptolysin O, M protein**); that difference is what Centor scores.

steps.q: Which mechanism explains rheumatic fever weeks after untreated strep throat?
o: Direct bacterial invasion of the heart
Immune complex deposition in the skin
steps.r: Antibodies against streptococcal antigens such as **M protein** cross-react with heart, joint and brain tissue: **molecular mimicry**.

steps.title: Untreated strep throat to rheumatic fever
nodes: Cross-reaction with cardiac myosin and valves

steps.lead: Treating Ellie's strep throat reduces her risk of **rheumatic fever** and **post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis**, both from **molecular mimicry** weeks later.
Ellie's infection broke through the tonsillar capsule; the inflamed **pterygoid muscles** next door went into spasm, giving her **trismus**.

steps.text: Post-strep glomerulonephritis comes **1-3 weeks** after the throat infection; IgA nephropathy gives haematuria **within days** of it.

mcq.q: Which organism most commonly causes bacterial tonsillitis?
Which is NOT one of the Centor criteria?
mcq.r: The fourth criterion is **tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy**; splenomegaly suggests glandular fever.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests a peritonsillar abscess?
mcq.r: **Trismus**, hot potato voice and a one-sided peritonsillar swelling are quinsy.
Most common in **children and young adults**.

mcq.q: Which test confirms Group A strep tonsillitis?
mcq.r: A **throat swab** confirms GAS when bacterial infection is suspected.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is used for tonsillitis in penicillin allergy?
How many episodes in the last 12 months meet the SIGN tonsillectomy criterion?
mcq.r: **7+** in 1 year, 5+ in each of 2 years, or 3+ in each of 3 years.

mcq.q: A patient on atorvastatin needs clarithromycin. What should you do with the statin?
mcq.r: **Hold the statin**: clarithromycin raises its level and risks rhabdomyolysis.

mcq.q: Which mechanism causes rheumatic fever after strep throat?
mcq.r: **Molecular mimicry** between streptococcal antigens and human tissue.

mcq.q: Which muscles cause trismus in quinsy?
mcq.r: Inflammation and spasm of the **pterygoid muscles**.

technique.stem: A 17 year old boy has a 2 day history of a severe sore throat and painful swallowing. He has no cough. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. Both tonsils are enlarged with white exudate, and he has tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. There is no splenomegaly.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a sore throat: count Centor and look for the look-alikes.
All four **Centor** criteria; no splenomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Centor 4: **bacterial (Group A strep) tonsillitis**.

elim: Diphtheria: grey adherent membrane, unvaccinated, very rare in the UK.
Glandular fever: splenomegaly and posterior nodes.
Quinsy is one-sided with trismus and uvula deviation.
Viral pharyngitis usually has cough and coryza.

steps.x: **A. Bacterial tonsillitis.** Centor 4 = likely Group A strep.

technique.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 3 day history of a sore throat and fever. She has no cough. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Both tonsils have exudate and she has tender anterior cervical nodes. Her GP wants to confirm whether the infection is caused by Group A Streptococcus.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: The question asks how to **confirm Group A strep** now.

clues: confirm whether the infection is caused by Group A Streptococcus
steps.x: Acute bacterial tonsillitis suspected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **throat swab** confirms GAS.

elim: ASO titre shows past infection, used for rheumatic fever or post-strep GN.
Blood cultures are rarely positive in tonsillitis.
CT neck is for deep neck abscess, not simple tonsillitis.
Monospot tests for EBV, not strep.

steps.x: **E. Throat swab.** Clinical diagnosis; swab confirms GAS.

technique.stem: A 5 year old boy has a 3 day history of sore throat and fever. He has refused all drinks for 2 days and has passed very little urine. He is lethargic. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 150 bpm and capillary refill time 4 seconds. His tonsils are enlarged with exudate. He has a cough.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: is this child safe at home?
**Dehydrated** and systemically unwell.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Systemically unwell child: Centor irrelevant, **immediate admission**.

elim: He needs fluids and assessment, not oral antibiotics at home.
Home self-care is unsafe when dehydrated.
Oral antibiotics at home ignore the dehydration.
Waiting for a swab delays urgent care.

steps.x: **B. Immediate hospital admission.** Unwell or dehydrated child = admit, whatever the score.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has had left-sided throat pain for 5 days after tonsillitis. He now cannot open his mouth more than one finger's width. His voice is muffled. There is a tender swelling above the left tonsil pushing the uvula to the right.
technique.q: Which is the most likely cause of his difficulty opening his mouth?

steps.x: Mechanism of trismus in this patient.

clues: cannot open his mouth more than one finger's width
tender swelling above the left tonsil
pushing the uvula to the right
steps.x: **Quinsy** with trismus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection in the peritonsillar space inflames the nearby **pterygoid muscles**, causing spasm.

elim: TMJ dislocation follows trauma or yawning, not infection.
CN XII palsy causes tongue deviation, not trismus.
The collection is peritonsillar, not in the masseter.
Tetanus follows a wound and causes generalised spasm.

steps.x: **D. Spasm of the pterygoid muscles.** Quinsy trismus = pterygoid irritation.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman has a 2 day history of a sore throat and pain on swallowing. She has no cough or runny nose. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Both tonsils are red with pus on them. She has tender lymph nodes at the angle of the jaw. Her abdomen is soft with no organomegaly.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes and no cough give Centor 4: bacterial tonsillitis. No organomegaly makes glandular fever less likely; no trismus rules out quinsy.

steps.x: Sore throat diagnosis: score Centor.

clues: tender lymph nodes at the angle of the jaw
steps.x: **Centor 4**, no splenomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Group A strep **bacterial tonsillitis**.

elim: Epiglottitis: drooling, stridor, tripod position.
Glandular fever: splenomegaly, posterior nodes, fatigue.
Quinsy: one-sided, trismus, uvula deviation.
Viral pharyngitis usually has cough and coryza.

steps.x: **B. Bacterial tonsillitis.** Four Centor criteria.

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has had tonsillitis for 4 days. Today the pain is much worse on the right and he cannot open his mouth fully. His voice sounds muffled and he is drooling. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. The uvula is deviated to the left.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: One-sided pain, trismus, hot potato voice and uvula deviation away from the side after tonsillitis is quinsy. Ludwig's angina is floor-of-mouth swelling from a dental source.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication of tonsillitis.

clues: uvula is deviated to the left
steps.x: One-sided, **trismus**, **hot potato voice**, uvula pushed away.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**.

elim: Epiglottitis causes stridor and no uvula deviation.
Glandular fever is bilateral, with splenomegaly.
Ludwig's angina: floor-of-mouth swelling from a tooth.
Retropharyngeal abscess is in young children with neck stiffness.

steps.x: **D. Peritonsillar abscess.** Trismus + uvula deviation after tonsillitis = quinsy.

practice.stem: A 14 year old girl has a 3 day history of sore throat and fever. She has no cough. Her temperature is 38.8°C. Both tonsils are covered in exudate and her anterior cervical nodes are tender. A throat swab grows beta-haemolytic colonies on blood agar.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Bacterial tonsillitis is caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), which is beta-haemolytic. S. pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic.

steps.x: Organism question.
Centor 4 and a **beta-haemolytic** organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Group A Streptococcus: Streptococcus pyogenes**.

elim: EBV is a virus and does not grow on blood agar.
H. influenzae causes epiglottitis and otitis media.
S. aureus is not a usual tonsillitis cause.
S. pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pyogenes.** Bacterial tonsillitis = Group A strep.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has a sore throat for 2 days. He has a dry cough. His temperature is 37.8°C. Both tonsils are red and covered in white exudate. He has tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
practice.e: He scores for exudate and tender anterior nodes only. A cough loses a point and 37.8°C is not above 38°C: Centor 2.

steps.x: Count each of the four Centor criteria.
Exudate (1), nodes (1); fever not above 38°C (0); cough present (0).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **2 points**: low to intermediate probability of Group A strep.

elim: He has two positive criteria.
Do not miss the tender anterior nodes.
37.8°C does not score: the cut-off is above 38°C.
A cough and a low-grade fever each lose a point.

steps.x: **C. 2.** Check the exact temperature and the cough every time.

practice.stem: An 8 year old boy had a sore throat with fever 2 days ago. He now has a rough, sandpaper-like red rash starting on his neck and chest, flushed cheeks with pallor around his mouth, and a red swollen tongue. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication of his tonsillitis?
practice.e: Sandpaper rash, circumoral pallor and strawberry tongue after strep throat is scarlet fever, a complication in the notes. Rheumatic fever comes weeks later with joints and carditis.

steps.x: A complication of strep tonsillitis: timing and rash.

clues: sore throat with fever 2 days ago
steps.x: Classic **scarlet fever** features within days.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Group A strep toxin rash: **scarlet fever**.

elim: Measles has cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
Rheumatic fever is 2-4 weeks later with carditis and arthritis.
Toxic shock causes hypotension and shock; BP is normal.
Varicella gives itchy vesicles in crops, not a sandpaper rash.

steps.x: **C. Scarlet fever.** Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue after strep throat.

practice.stem: A 21 year old woman has a severe sore throat for 2 days with fever and no cough. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Both tonsils are enlarged with white exudate.
practice.q: Which additional finding on examination is most likely?
practice.e: Bacterial tonsillitis gives tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, a Centor criterion. Splenomegaly and generalised nodes suggest glandular fever.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question for bacterial tonsillitis.
Three Centor criteria already: this is **bacterial tonsillitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The remaining Centor sign: **tender anterior cervical nodes**.

elim: Generalised nodes suggest EBV or HIV.
Koplik spots are measles.
Splenomegaly is glandular fever.
Stridor suggests croup or epiglottitis.

steps.x: **E. Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.** The fourth Centor criterion.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has a 3 day history of sore throat and fever. He has no cough. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Both tonsils have exudate and there are tender anterior cervical nodes. The GP wants to confirm the bacterial cause.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: A throat swab confirms Group A strep when a bacterial cause is suspected. ASO titre reflects past infection and is used for post-streptococcal complications.

steps.x: Confirming the organism in acute tonsillitis.
Centor 4; the GP wants confirmation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Throat swab** for Group A strep.

elim: ASO rises over weeks; used for rheumatic fever.
No chest signs.
FBC may show neutrophilia but does not identify the organism.
Monospot is for EBV.

steps.x: **E. Throat swab.** It confirms GAS.

practice.stem: A 16 year old girl has tonsillitis with fever and exudate and no cough. Her temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. Blood tests are taken.
practice.q: Which blood result would most support a bacterial cause?
practice.e: Bacterial tonsillitis may show raised white cells (neutrophils) and CRP. Atypical lymphocytes and lymphocytosis point to glandular fever.

steps.x: Which result fits bacterial infection?

clues: fever and exudate and no cough
steps.x: High Centor: likely bacterial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bacterial infection: **raised WCC (neutrophils) and CRP**.

elim: Atypical lymphocytes are EBV.
Low platelets are not typical of strep.
Lymphocytosis suggests a viral cause.
Eosinophilia suggests allergy or parasites.

steps.x: **D. Neutrophilia with raised CRP.** Bacterial = neutrophils up.

practice.stem: A 20 year old woman has a 2 day history of severe sore throat with no cough. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Both tonsils have exudate and she has tender anterior cervical nodes. She is drinking fluids. She has no drug allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Centor 4 (above 3) means oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5-10 days. Amoxicillin is avoided because of the rash if the cause is EBV.

steps.x: Management: score Centor, check allergy.
**Centor 4**, not allergic, drinking.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Phenoxymethylpenicillin** (penicillin V).

elim: Amoxicillin causes a rash in glandular fever.
Clarithromycin is for penicillin allergy.
Self-care alone is for a low Centor.
One episode does not meet SIGN criteria.

steps.x: **D. Phenoxymethylpenicillin.** High Centor, no allergy.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has bacterial tonsillitis with a Centor score of 4. He is allergic to penicillin. He takes atorvastatin 40 mg daily, ramipril and aspirin. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Clarithromycin is the penicillin-allergy choice, but it inhibits statin metabolism and raises rhabdomyolysis risk, so hold atorvastatin during the course.

steps.x: Two decisions: antibiotic and drug interaction.
Needs an antibiotic, cannot have penicillin, on a statin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clarithromycin and hold the statin.**

elim: Amoxicillin is a penicillin.
Continuing the statin risks rhabdomyolysis.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin; aspirin is not the problem.
Penicillin V is contraindicated by the allergy.

steps.x: **C. Clarithromycin and hold atorvastatin.**

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has a left peritonsillar abscess after 5 days of tonsillitis. She has trismus and a hot potato voice. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Her airway is patent and oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Quinsy is treated with drainage (needle aspiration or incision) plus antibiotics, with corticosteroids as an adjunct. Antibiotics alone do not drain the pus.

steps.x: Management of quinsy.

clues: trismus and a hot potato voice
steps.x: An established **abscess**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pus needs **drainage plus antibiotics**.

elim: Tonsillectomy may follow later but does not treat the acute abscess.
Antibiotics alone do not drain pus.
Steroids are only an adjunct.
Delay risks airway compromise and spread.

steps.x: **A. Drainage and antibiotics.** Abscess = drain it.

practice.stem: A 12 year old boy had an untreated sore throat with fever 3 weeks ago. He now has painful swelling of the knees then the ankles, a new murmur and raised antistreptolysin O titre. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his current illness?
o: Direct bacterial infection of the joints
practice.e: Rheumatic fever after untreated Group A strep tonsillitis is caused by molecular mimicry: antibodies to streptococcal M protein cross-react with heart and joint tissue.

steps.x: Mechanism of a delayed complication.

clues: untreated sore throat with fever 3 weeks ago
steps.x: Weeks after strep throat: migratory arthritis and carditis = **rheumatic fever**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cross-reacting antibodies: **molecular mimicry**.

elim: The joints are sterile in rheumatic fever.
Exotoxins cause scarlet fever or toxic shock, not weeks-later arthritis.
This is not an allergic reaction.
Septic emboli suggest endocarditis with positive cultures.

steps.x: **D. Molecular mimicry.** Weeks after GAS = cross-reacting antibodies.

glossary.Tonsillitis: Infection and inflammation of the palatine tonsils.
glossary.Palatine tonsils: The two lymphoid lumps either side of the back of the throat.
glossary.Waldeyer's ring: The ring of lymphoid tissue (adenoids, palatine and lingual tonsils) guarding the throat.
glossary.Group A Streptococcus: Streptococcus pyogenes, the bacterium behind bacterial tonsillitis, scarlet fever and rheumatic fever.
glossary.Streptococcus pyogenes: The species name of Group A Streptococcus; beta-haemolytic on blood agar.
glossary.Beta-haemolytic: Bacteria that completely break down red cells on blood agar, leaving a clear zone.
glossary.Exudate: Pus or fluid coating the surface of inflamed tonsils, seen as white patches.
glossary.Cervical lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck.
glossary.Centor criteria: Four-point score (exudate, tender anterior nodes, fever over 38°C, no cough) estimating the chance of Group A strep.
glossary.Centor: Short for the Centor criteria, the sore throat score used to decide antibiotics.
glossary.FeverPAIN: An alternative sore throat score: fever, purulence, fast attendance, inflamed tonsils, no cough or coryza.
glossary.Quinsy: Peritonsillar abscess: a collection of pus beside the tonsil.
glossary.Peritonsillar abscess: Pus between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles, causing trismus and a hot potato voice.
glossary.Trismus: Difficulty opening the mouth because of jaw muscle spasm.
glossary.Hot potato voice: A muffled voice, as if speaking with a hot potato in the mouth, typical of quinsy.
glossary.Uvula: The small fleshy tag hanging from the soft palate; pushed away from a quinsy.
glossary.Pterygoid muscles: Jaw muscles near the tonsil; their spasm causes trismus in quinsy.
glossary.Rheumatic fever: Immune reaction 2-4 weeks after Group A strep throat, affecting heart, joints, skin and brain.
glossary.Scarlet fever: Group A strep infection with a sandpaper rash, flushed cheeks and strawberry tongue.
glossary.Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Kidney inflammation 1-3 weeks after strep infection, causing haematuria, oedema and hypertension.
glossary.Molecular mimicry: When antibodies made against a microbe also attack similar-looking human tissue.
glossary.M protein: A Group A strep surface protein; antibodies against it cross-react with heart tissue.
glossary.Streptolysin O: A Group A strep toxin that damages cells; antibodies to it (ASO titre) show recent infection.
glossary.ASO titre: Antistreptolysin O antibody level, showing recent Group A strep infection.
glossary.Antistreptolysin O titre: Blood test for antibodies to streptolysin O, showing recent strep infection.
glossary.Throat swab: A swab of the tonsils sent for culture to identify Group A strep.
glossary.Monospot: Rapid test for heterophile antibodies in glandular fever (EBV).
glossary.Infectious mononucleosis: Glandular fever: EBV infection with sore throat, posterior nodes, fatigue and splenomegaly.
glossary.Glandular fever: Infectious mononucleosis, caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
glossary.EBV: Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever.
glossary.Phenoxymethylpenicillin: Penicillin V: the first-line oral antibiotic for strep tonsillitis.
glossary.Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic for penicillin allergy; it raises statin levels.
glossary.Rhabdomyolysis: Breakdown of skeletal muscle releasing myoglobin, which can cause kidney injury.
glossary.Atorvastatin: A statin that lowers cholesterol; its level rises dangerously with clarithromycin.
glossary.Tonsillectomy: Surgical removal of the palatine tonsils.
glossary.Diphtheria: Rare toxin-producing infection with a grey adherent throat membrane, in unvaccinated people.
glossary.Epiglottitis: Infection of the epiglottis causing drooling, stridor and airway risk.
glossary.SIGN criteria: Scottish (SIGN) tonsillectomy criteria: 7+ episodes in 1 year, 5+ in each of 2 years, or 3+ in each of 3 years.
